name: Enggano
confidence_why: Kähler's 1940 grammar, the only first-hand description of pre-war Enggano, puts the accent on the penultimate syllable and Crowley (n.d.), Edwards (2015) and Hemmings & Arka (2023) all repeat him, but Yoder (2011), the one modern first-hand phonological study, finds stress consistently on the final syllable and takes the difference to be a change in the language since the 1930s.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Enggano usually falls on the penultimate syllable (Kähler 1940:84), though it occasionally falls elsewhere: notably, stress is antepenultimate when vowel leak has occurred. [p. 60] ... a vowel before either of the glottal consonants /ʔ/ or /h/ will "leak" across the consonant and be found after the glottal as well, so long as the preglottal and postglottal vowels are of different qualities. Such vowels carry no weight for the purposes of assigning stress (see below) and often form a diphthong with the following vowel. [p. 59] ... I follow Kähler in marking nonpenultimate stress with an acute accent. [p. 60]
new_statements.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2015. The position of Enggano within Austronesian. Oceanic Linguistics 54(1): 54-109.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (57 pp., Project Muse producer, title 'The Position of Enggano within Austronesian', author Owen Edwards). extracted text pages 7-8 (journal pp. 59-60): p. 60 reads exactly 'Stress in Enggano usually falls on the penultimate syllable (Kähler 1940:84), though it occasionally falls elsewhere: notably, stress is antepenultimate when vowel leak has occurred.'; p. 59 (§2.2.1.3 Suprasegmental features) reads exactly '.. a vowel before either of the glottal consonants /ʔ/ or /h/ will "leak" across the consonant and be found after the glottal as well, so long as the preglottal and postglottal vowels are of different qualities. Such vowels carry no weight for the purposes of assigning stress…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's StressTyp2 penultimate rule (penultimate stress); adds the weight-of-leaked-vowel exception producing surface antepenultimate stress and the source (Kähler 1940:84).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is normally on the penultimate syllable. A vowel copied ('leaked') across /ʔ/ or /h/ onto the following vowel does not count for stress assignment, so words with vowel leak surface with antepenultimate stress (e.g. e-adá-ʔau̯ 'my child', e-báhau̯ 'heart'). Non-penultimate stress is marked with an acute accent in Edwards's transcription; penultimate stress is left unmarked.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress when vowel leak has occurred (obligatory in some morphemes such as the 1sg genitive suffix -ʔVu, historical in lexemes like e-báhau̯ 'heart', optional in others such as ẽ-ã́hĩ ~ ẽ-ã́hãĩ̯ 'younger brother'). The statement is explicitly taken from Kähler 1940:84, i.e. Enggano as recorded in 1937-38.
new_statements.identity_note: Edwards 2015 (pp. 55-57) and Crowley (§3.1) both describe the Enggano recorded by Kähler in 1937-38, when only one dialect (the northern one, spoken on the north coast after the collapse of the earlier eastern/western or northern/southern/western dialects) survived; the stress statements therefore describe that 1930s variety. Hemmings et al. 2023 describe Contemporary Enggano (2018 onward) but say nothing about its stress.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Enggano is apparently penultimate, and when a word is suffixed there is a backward shifting of stress to the surface penultimate syllable in the word. However, Kähler says that when a suffix is one of a small group of particular possessive suffixes, irregular stress patterns are encountered. E.g. stem: úba 'house' suffixed forms: eúbadia 'his house' eúbadai 'our house' eúbadu 'your pl. house' eubákaPa 'our house' [p. 6] With these four irregular suffixes, we find that we have instead antepenultimate stress. [p. 7] ... Several vowels can occur in sequence, though word finally a sequence of two vowels is regarded as a single unit for the purposes of stress placement. Thus in eubadia and eubadai above, the sequences -ia and -ai are treated as belonging to a single syllable for the placement of stress (which in these words is antepenultimate as explained above). [p. 7, §3.4]
new_statements.citation: Crowley, Terry (n.d.). Grammatical sketch of Enggano.
new_statements.locator: §3.3 Stress, pp. 6-7, and §3.4 Phonotactics, p. 7 (pp. 6-7 of the transcription)

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's penultimate placement and adds the suffix-induced antepenultimate exceptions and the final-VV-as-one-syllable rule; secondary source derived from Kähler 1940, like Edwards.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is penultimate and shifts rightward onto the new penultimate syllable when suffixes are added; four possessive suffixes (-dia, -dai, -du, -kaʔa) are irregular and leave stress on the antepenult; a word-final two-vowel sequence counts as one syllable for stress placement (so the -dia/-dai cases are antepenultimate by vowel count but penultimate by that syllabification).
new_statements.exceptions: Four irregular possessive suffixes (3sg -dia, 1pl.excl -dai, 2pl -du, 1pl.incl -kaʔa) give antepenultimate stress; final VV counts as one syllable for stress. Crowley states he is reporting Kähler (1940); the preface notes the sketch was written mainly from Kähler's 1940 grammar and that the transcription of a hard-to-read photocopy may contain inaccuracies.
new_statements.identity_note: Edwards 2015 (pp. 55-57) and Crowley (§3.1) both describe the Enggano recorded by Kähler in 1937-38, when only one dialect (the northern one, spoken on the north coast after the collapse of the earlier eastern/western or northern/southern/western dialects) survived; the stress statements therefore describe that 1930s variety. Hemmings et al. 2023 describe Contemporary Enggano (2018 onward) but say nothing about its stress.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement: the two works that discuss stress (Edwards 2015 p. 60; Crowley n.d. pp. 6-7) both state penultimate word stress and both trace it to Kähler 1940:84. They describe the antepenultimate exceptions differently: Crowley attributes them to four irregular possessive suffixes (-dia, -dai, -du, -kaʔa) and notes that a word-final vowel sequence counts as one syllable, while Edwards attributes them to vowel leak across /ʔ/ and /h/ (the leaked vowel carries no weight). These are compatible readings of the same Kähler data (e.g. Crowley's eubákaPa and Edwards's e-adá-ʔau̯ both involve a glottal followed by a copied vowel), not a contradiction. Hemmings et al. 2023 is silent on stress. No source mentions secondary stress, and none gives an independent, instrumental or contemporary account: everything rests on Kähler's 1937-38 description.

audit.recode_to: Contemporary Enggano (the living language under engg1245): fixed final stress, final stress, secondary stress alternating right-to-left, per Yoder 2011:37 (instrumental). If the record is meant to describe Kähler's 1930s 'Old Enggano' doculect instead, keep penultimate but drop 'strict' (Kähler: 'generally'; suffixed forms 'sometimes' keep original stress; enclitics =dia/=dai/=du leave stress pre-penultimate, e.g. eúbadia — Kähler 1940:96 via Hemmings & Arka 2023) and add a caution that the modern language has final stress. Either way add Yoder 2011 as a contra/caution.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim on p. 6 of the held Burleigh & Dalrymple translation of Kähler 1940, as cited. (2) The deciding source is a 1940 grammar sketch of 1937-38 Enggano whose stress statement is hedged ('generally', 'often.. but sometimes'), yet the catalog codes 'fixed-strict' penultimate. (3) The best available stress description, Yoder 2011 (Glottolog's first-ranked phonology ref, 147 pp, acoustic measurements, downloaded now), states that stress in Enggano as spoken today is consistently word-final in mono- and polymorphemic words and in loans, and explicitly notes the change from Kähler's penultimate pattern; the 1895 Holle list already reported penultimate-or-final. Hemmings & Arka 2023 (downloaded) confirm for Old Enggano that certain enclitics did not shift stress, so even the 1940 doculect was not 'strict'. (4) Hence at-risk: a better, held-as-of-now so

In Enggano this generally lies on the vowel of the penultimate syllable. If a word is extended by suffixes, the accent is often placed on the vowel of the penultimate syllable, but sometimes remains on the original syllable.' Identical in lines 250-254. sources.quote: For Old Enggano (restating Kähler 1940:96): 'In most cases, the process of suffixation triggers stress shift, so that the stress is on the penultimate syllable. However, the enclitics =dia, =dai and =du do not trigger this same process, with stress remaining on the [u] vowel' (eúbadia, eúbadai, eúbadu). No statement on contemporary stress position; notes vowel reduction 'in non-stressed syllables' and regular final-vowel loss in Contemporary Enggano.

tone.quote: Yoder (2011ː 38) shows that stress correlates with duration and pitch. Intensity does not correlate with stress, though there does appear to be a difference in intensity between closed final syllables and open final syllables.
